title: Peritoneum & Foregut Organs
summary: Learn how the peritoneum wraps the abdominal organs and study the stomach, duodenum, liver, biliary tree, pancreas and spleen.

lessons.title: Peritoneal Cavity: Greater Sac, Lesser Sac and Omental Foramen

levels.kid:
Imagine your tummy organs are wrapped in a thin, slippery plastic bag. That bag is called the **peritoneum**. It is wet and smooth, so your stomach and intestines can slide around when you eat and move.

The bag has two rooms. The big room is called the **greater sac**. It holds most of your tummy organs. The small room hides behind your stomach. It is called the **lesser sac**.

The two rooms are joined by a tiny doorway, just big enough for one finger. Doctors call it the **omental foramen**. Surgeons know exactly where this little door is. It sits right next to important tubes that carry blood and juices to the liver.
levels.hs:
The **peritoneum** is a thin, slippery membrane lining the abdomen. It has two layers. The **parietal peritoneum** lines the inside of the abdominal wall. The **visceral peritoneum** covers the surface of organs. Between them is the **peritoneal cavity**. This is a potential space: normally it holds only a thin film of fluid that lets organs glide.

The cavity has two parts:
- **Greater sac**: the main space, holding most of the cavity.
- **Lesser sac** (also called the **omental bursa**): a smaller pocket behind the stomach and the lesser omentum.

The two sacs connect through the **omental foramen**, also called the **epiploic foramen** or the foramen of Winslow. It is a slit about the width of a finger.

Two folds of peritoneum, called **omenta**, hang from the stomach:
- The **greater omentum** drapes down from the stomach's greater curvature like an apron over the intestines.
- The **lesser omentum** runs from the stomach's lesser curvature to the liver.

A real example: if a patient has a perforated ulcer on the back wall of the stomach, stomach contents can leak into the lesser sac. Fluid can then pass through the omental foramen into the greater sac.

In people assigned male at birth the cavity is fully closed. In people assigned female at birth it opens to the outside through the uterine tubes.
levels.college:
The peritoneum is a serous membrane of mesothelium on loose connective tissue. Its innervation differs by layer:
- **Parietal peritoneum**: somatic nerves (lower intercostal, subcostal, iliohypogastric, ilioinguinal and phrenic), so pain from it is sharp and well localized.
- **Visceral peritoneum**: autonomic afferents, so pain from it is dull and poorly localized.

**Organ relationships**
- **Intraperitoneal** organs are almost fully covered and hang on a mesentery. Examples are the stomach, the first part of the duodenum, the jejunum, the ileum and the spleen.
- **Retroperitoneal** organs lie behind the cavity. They are either primary (the kidneys) or secondarily retroperitoneal because they fused to the posterior wall during development (most of the duodenum, the pancreas, and the ascending and descending colon).

**Lesser omentum**: this has two parts, the **hepatogastric ligament** and the **hepatoduodenal ligament**. The free right edge of the hepatoduodenal ligament carries the **portal triad**: the bile duct (right, anterior), the hepatic artery proper (left, anterior) and the hepatic portal vein (posterior).

**Boundaries of the omental (epiploic) foramen**
- Anterior: the hepatoduodenal ligament and the portal triad
- Posterior: the inferior vena cava and the right crus of the diaphragm
- Superior: the caudate lobe of the liver
- Inferior: the first part of the duodenum

**Lesser sac relations**: in front of the sac lie the stomach and lesser omentum. Behind it is the stomach bed: pancreas, left kidney and suprarenal gland, splenic artery and transverse mesocolon. To the left it is closed by the gastrosplenic and splenorenal ligaments.

**Greater sac subdivisions**: the transverse mesocolon divides the greater sac into **supracolic** and **infracolic compartments**. Paracolic gutters run beside the ascending and descending colon. In the supine position, the **hepatorenal recess (Morison's pouch)** is the lowest part of the upper abdomen, so fluid collects there.
levels.phd:
The peritoneal anatomy of the adult is best understood through development. The gut tube is first suspended in a ventral and dorsal mesogastrium. Between about weeks 5 and 6, the stomach rotates 90 degrees clockwise when viewed from above, around a longitudinal axis. This swings the dorsal mesogastrium to the left and creates the lesser sac as a recess behind the stomach. The ventral mesogastrium, invaded by the growing liver, becomes the lesser omentum and the falciform ligament. The dorsal mesogastrium balloons downward as the greater omentum, a four-layered fold. Its posterior layers fuse with the transverse mesocolon, so the adult lesser sac usually stops above the transverse colon. The inferior recess between the omental layers is mostly obliterated in adults.

Secondary retroperitonealization happens by fusion of visceral and parietal peritoneum, forming avascular **fusion fascias**. Examples are the fascia of Toldt behind the colon and the fascia of Treitz behind the pancreas and duodenum. These planes explain why mobilizing the colon or the pancreaticoduodenal unit (the Kocher manoeuvre) can be done almost bloodlessly.

Peritoneal fluid flows in predictable directions. Diaphragmatic movement creates negative subphrenic pressure, which draws fluid upward along the right paracolic gutter. The phrenicocolic ligament limits flow up the left gutter. Classic radiological work by Meyers described these routes and explains why infection spreads from the appendix to the right subphrenic and hepatorenal spaces.

Peritoneal absorption happens mainly through specialized **stomata** of the diaphragmatic mesothelium. These drain into subdiaphragmatic lymphatics, then into parasternal and mediastinal nodes, which is why particles reach the thorax.

The greater omentum contains **milky spots**: aggregates of macrophages and lymphocytes around glomerulus-like capillary networks (omental glomeruli). They help the omentum wall off inflamed viscera, a role that earned it the nickname "policeman of the abdomen". The same milky spots also host early peritoneal metastases, especially in ovarian and gastric cancer.
levels.expert:
Clinically, the omental foramen matters most for the **Pringle manoeuvre**. A finger is passed through the foramen and the hepatoduodenal ligament is clamped, which stops hepatic artery and portal inflow. This is used to control bleeding from the liver in trauma and during resection. If bleeding continues after a correct Pringle, the source is likely the hepatic veins or retrohepatic inferior vena cava, or an aberrant left hepatic artery running in the hepatogastric ligament, which the clamp does not cover. The posterior wall of the foramen is the IVC, so blind or forceful dissection there is dangerous.

Access to the lesser sac is gained in three main ways:
- through the gastrocolic ligament, the standard route for pancreatic necrosectomy and for inspecting the posterior gastric wall
- through the lesser omentum, which risks an aberrant left hepatic artery or the left gastric vessels
- through the transverse mesocolon in a chosen avascular window

Necrotizing pancreatitis now favours a step-up approach, often endoscopic transgastric drainage of walled-off necrosis, over open necrosectomy.

**Internal hernias** can occur through the omental foramen. They are rare but dangerous, and are usually linked to a mobile right colon or a long mesentery. CT shows bowel posterior to the portal triad, with a gas-filled loop wedged between the IVC and portal vein.

Key imaging relations:
- **Morison's pouch** is the first window checked on FAST ultrasound for free fluid in blunt trauma.
- The rectovesical or rectouterine pouch is the most dependent site when the patient is upright.

In peritoneal carcinomatosis, the **Peritoneal Cancer Index** scores 13 regions to guide cytoreductive surgery with HIPEC (hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy). Omentectomy is standard because of milky-spot seeding. **Peritoneal dialysis** relies on the large, semipermeable membrane, but long-term exposure can lead to encapsulating peritoneal sclerosis.

Open questions include:
- the biology of mesothelial-to-mesenchymal transition in adhesions and metastasis
- whether the mesentery should count as a continuous organ, a framing promoted by Coffey's work and relevant to complete mesocolic excision in colorectal surgery

test.q: The lesser sac lies mainly posterior to which structure?
test.explain: The lesser sac (omental bursa) is a recess behind the stomach and lesser omentum. The left kidney lies behind the sac, not in front of it.

test.q: What forms the posterior boundary of the omental foramen?
test.explain: The IVC (with the right crus of the diaphragm) lies behind the foramen. The portal vein lies in front of it, inside the hepatoduodenal ligament.

test.q: Which structure forms the superior boundary of the omental foramen?
test.explain: The caudate lobe of the liver roofs the foramen. The duodenum forms its floor.

test.q: The free edge of the hepatoduodenal ligament carries the:
test.explain: The portal triad (bile duct, hepatic artery proper, portal vein) runs in the free edge and forms the anterior wall of the foramen.

test.q: Why is pain from the parietal peritoneum well localized?
choices: It lies close to the skin surface
It is supplied by the vagus nerve
It has no autonomic nerve fibers
It is supplied by somatic nerves
test.explain: Parietal peritoneum has somatic innervation (for example the intercostal and phrenic nerves), giving sharp, localized pain. Visceral peritoneum's autonomic supply gives vague pain.

test.q: Which organ is secondarily retroperitoneal?
test.explain: The pancreas becomes retroperitoneal by fusing with the posterior wall. The kidney is primarily retroperitoneal, and the spleen and stomach are intraperitoneal.

test.q: In a patient lying supine, where does free fluid in the upper abdomen tend to collect?
test.explain: The hepatorenal recess (Morison's pouch) is the lowest part of the upper abdomen in the supine position.

test.q: The greater omentum hangs from the stomach's:
test.explain: The greater omentum drapes down from the greater curvature like an apron. The lesser omentum attaches to the lesser curvature.

test.q: Which structure divides the greater sac into supracolic and infracolic compartments?
test.explain: The transverse mesocolon forms a horizontal shelf that separates the upper and lower compartments of the greater sac.

test.q: Give the eponym for the omental (epiploic) foramen: the foramen of ___.
test.explain: It is named after the anatomist Jacob Winslow.

test.q: The lesser sac is also called the omental ___.
test.explain: 'Omental bursa' is the formal name for the lesser sac.

test.q: The layer of peritoneum that covers the surface of organs is the ___ peritoneum.
test.explain: Visceral peritoneum covers the organs. Parietal peritoneum lines the abdominal wall.

kidTest.q: Which room holds most of the tummy organs?
kidTest.explain: The big room, called the greater sac, holds most of them.

kidTest.q: Where does the lesser sac hide?
kidTest.explain: The small room sits behind the stomach.

advancedTest.q: Bleeding from the liver continues despite a correct Pringle manoeuvre. Which source is most likely?
choices: The hepatic veins or retrohepatic IVC
The portal vein in the free edge
The proper hepatic artery in the triad
The common bile duct in the ligament
advancedTest.explain: The Pringle clamp stops inflow through the portal triad. Bleeding from outflow vessels (hepatic veins, retrohepatic IVC) is not controlled by it.

advancedTest.q: Why does infection from the appendix tend to reach the right subphrenic space?
choices: The lesser sac drains directly toward the appendix
Negative subphrenic pressure draws fluid up the right gutter
The phrenicocolic ligament guides fluid up the right side
The transverse mesocolon funnels fluid to the right side
advancedTest.explain: Diaphragmatic movement creates negative subphrenic pressure, which draws fluid up the right paracolic gutter. The phrenicocolic ligament limits spread on the left, not the right.

advancedTest.q: Why does the adult lesser sac usually stop above the transverse colon?
choices: The falciform ligament blocks spread of the sac downward
The stomach's rotation pulls the sac upward toward the liver
The lesser omentum grows down and seals the sac below
Posterior omental layers fuse with the transverse mesocolon
advancedTest.explain: The posterior layers of the greater omentum fuse with the transverse mesocolon. This fusion obliterates most of the lower recess of the sac.

advancedTest.q: Why can a Kocher manoeuvre mobilize the duodenum with little bleeding?
choices: The duodenum lacks any arterial supply in that region
The portal triad is clamped first in this procedure
It follows an avascular fusion fascia plane
The lesser sac cushions the vessels during dissection
advancedTest.explain: Secondary retroperitonealization forms avascular fusion fascias (here the fascia of Treitz). Surgeons dissect along these planes to mobilize organs almost bloodlessly.

lessons.title: Stomach and Duodenum: Parts, Relations and Blood Supply

levels.kid:
Your **stomach** is a stretchy bag shaped a bit like a letter J. It sits up near the top of your belly on the left side, tucked under your ribs. Food slides down a tube into the top of the bag. The stomach squeezes and mixes it with juices, like a washing machine churning clothes.

At the bottom of the J there is a tight ring of muscle, like the drawstring on a bag. It lets a little food out at a time into the **duodenum**. That is the first part of your small intestine, and it curls into a C shape.

Both need lots of blood to work. Small blood vessels hug their curved edges like vines on a fence, bringing food and oxygen to every part.
levels.hs:
The **stomach** is a J-shaped muscular sac in the upper left abdomen. It stores food, churns it, and starts digesting protein with acid and enzymes.

Its parts, from top to bottom:
- **Cardia**: where the esophagus enters.
- **Fundus**: the dome that bulges up under the left diaphragm. It often holds a gas bubble on X-rays.
- **Body**: the large middle part.
- **Pyloric part**: the narrowing end. The **pyloric sphincter**, a thick ring of smooth muscle, controls how fast food leaves.

The stomach has two curved edges. The inner edge is the short **lesser curvature**, and the outer edge is the long **greater curvature**.

The **duodenum** is the first part of the small intestine, about 25 cm long and shaped like a C. It wraps around the head of the pancreas. Bile from the liver and enzymes from the pancreas pour into it, so it is where most chemical digestion gets going.

Blood comes from the **celiac trunk**, a short artery off the aorta that supplies the upper gut. Its branches run along both curvatures of the stomach.

Real example: a **peptic ulcer** is a sore in the lining, often in the first part of the duodenum. If an ulcer erodes through the back wall of the duodenum, it can hit a large artery lying right behind it and cause serious bleeding.
levels.college:
**Stomach parts and features.** The stomach has a cardia, fundus, body and pyloric part. The pyloric part is subdivided into the **pyloric antrum**, the pyloric canal and the pylorus. The **angular incisure** is a notch on the lesser curvature that marks the junction of body and antrum. The lining forms **gastric rugae**, folds that flatten as the stomach fills. The **lesser omentum** attaches to the lesser curvature, and the **greater omentum** hangs from the greater curvature.

**Relations.**
- Anterior: left lobe of the liver, diaphragm and anterior abdominal wall.
- Posterior (the **stomach bed**, separated from the stomach by the lesser sac): pancreas, splenic artery, left kidney and suprarenal gland, spleen, left colic flexure and transverse mesocolon.

**Duodenum: four parts.**
- **Superior (D1)**: the first 2 cm, the **ampulla or duodenal cap**, is intraperitoneal and mobile. The rest of the duodenum is retroperitoneal. The gastroduodenal artery, common bile duct and portal vein pass behind D1.
- **Descending (D2)**: the bile duct and main pancreatic duct open at the **major duodenal papilla**, about 7–10 cm from the pylorus. The accessory duct opens at the minor papilla.
- **Horizontal (D3)**: crosses the IVC and aorta at about L3, with the superior mesenteric vessels passing in front.
- **Ascending (D4)**: rises to the **duodenojejunal flexure**, which is suspended by the **suspensory muscle (ligament of Treitz)**.

**Arterial supply (celiac trunk).**
- Lesser curvature: **left gastric** artery (from the celiac) and **right gastric** artery (usually from the proper or common hepatic artery).
- Greater curvature: **right gastro-omental** artery (from the gastroduodenal) and **left gastro-omental** artery (from the splenic).
- Fundus: **short gastric** arteries (from the splenic).
- Duodenum: superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries (from the gastroduodenal) and inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries (from the SMA). Their junction near the papilla marks the **foregut–midgut transition**.
levels.phd:
The stomach and proximal duodenum are foregut derivatives supplied by the celiac trunk. Distal to the major papilla, the duodenum is midgut, supplied by the SMA. The pancreaticoduodenal arcades join the two territories, which is the anatomical basis for collateral flow when the celiac origin is narrowed. Narrowing by the **median arcuate ligament** is a well-known cause, and in that setting the arcades may enlarge and form aneurysms.

**Gastric microcirculation.** The named arteries along each curvature form two marginal arcades. They pierce the muscularis and make a rich submucosal plexus, which is why the stomach is very resistant to ischaemia and can survive ligation of several of its main arteries. The lesser curvature has a less redundant intramural network, a feature proposed in classic work to explain why gastric ulcers tend to occur there and at the incisure.

**Venous drainage** parallels the arteries but ends in the hepatic portal system. The left gastric (coronary) vein connects with oesophageal veins that drain to the azygos system, forming the key **portosystemic anastomosis** that becomes oesophageal varices in portal hypertension. Short gastric veins drain to the splenic vein, so splenic vein thrombosis produces isolated gastric fundal varices.

**Functional regions** do not match the gross regions exactly. The fundus and body contain oxyntic glands with **parietal cells**, which secrete HCl via H+/K+-ATPase, and **chief cells**, which secrete pepsinogen. The antrum contains **G cells**, which secrete gastrin. The pylorus and duodenum use thickened circular muscle and neurohumoral feedback (CCK, secretin) to meter gastric emptying. **Brunner glands** in the D1 submucosa secrete alkaline mucus.

**Mobility and fixation.** D1 hangs on the hepatoduodenal ligament and is intraperitoneal, while D2–D4 became secondarily retroperitoneal when the mesoduodenum fused with the posterior wall. This fixation explains injury patterns: in blunt trauma, the retroperitoneal duodenum can be crushed against the vertebral column, as in handlebar injuries. The resulting retroperitoneal air or fluid may give few early peritoneal signs.

The **ligament of Treitz** is variably muscular and in places continuous with the right crus. Its exact composition is still debated, but it stays a central radiological landmark.
levels.expert:
Clinically, the vascular relations of the stomach and duodenum dominate decision-making in bleeding, oncology and imaging.

**Bleeding.** A posterior D1 ulcer can erode the **gastroduodenal artery**, causing major upper GI haemorrhage. Endoscopic therapy comes first. If it fails, surgical underrunning places sutures superiorly, inferiorly and medially, to control the GDA trunk and the transverse pancreatic branch. Alternatively, interventional radiologists perform transcatheter embolisation and must close both inflow sides, because collaterals from the SMA through the pancreaticoduodenal arcades can backfill the bleeding point. A lesser-curvature ulcer bleeds from left gastric branches. **Dieulafoy lesions**, abnormally large submucosal arteries, cluster in the proximal stomach along the lesser curvature.

**Oncology.** Gastric cancer staging and the extent of D2 lymphadenectomy follow the arteries. The Japanese Gastric Cancer Association numbers nodal stations along the left gastric, common hepatic, celiac and splenic arteries. Recognising the **aberrant left hepatic artery** from the left gastric (seen in roughly 10–20% of people) is essential, because dividing the left gastric at its origin can devascularise part of the liver. The right gastro-omental artery is preserved when the stomach is tubularised as an oesophageal conduit, since it becomes the conduit's main blood supply.

**Bariatric surgery** depends on these vessels. Sleeve gastrectomy divides the short gastrics, and staple-line leaks typically occur near the angle of His, where perfusion is poorest. A gastric bypass relies on a pouch built from the lesser curvature and fed by left gastric branches.

**Duodenal pitfalls.**
- **Superior mesenteric artery syndrome**: D3 is compressed in a narrowed aortomesenteric angle, often after rapid weight loss, for example following spinal fusion or prolonged neurosurgical illness. This is relevant to neurocritical-care patients who develop unexplained vomiting.
- The papilla's position varies. Periampullary diverticula complicate ERCP cannulation.
- In **malrotation**, the duodenojejunal flexure lies to the right of midline, and on contrast study a DJ flexure that does not reach the left pedicle at the level of the duodenal bulb suggests volvulus risk in infants.

**Open questions** include how reliably CT can quantify collateral arcade flow before Whipple surgery in patients with celiac stenosis, and whether a vascular origin for lesser-curvature ulcer predilection still matters in the Helicobacter-dominant era.

advancedTest.q: After embolising a bleeding gastroduodenal artery from above, rebleeding occurs. The most likely anatomical reason is:
choices: Venous bleeding from the portal vein behind the duodenal cap
Retrograde flow from the SMA through the pancreaticoduodenal arcades
Collateral flow from the left gastro-omental through the splenic vein
Backfilling from the left gastric artery through the short gastrics
advancedTest.explain: The pancreaticoduodenal arcades link celiac and SMA territories, so both inflow sides must be closed. The splenic vein is a vein and does not supply arterial collateral flow.

advancedTest.q: A patient with pancreatitis develops splenic vein thrombosis. Varices would most likely appear in the:
choices: Gastric fundus via the short gastric veins
Rectum via the superior rectal veins
Lower oesophagus via the left gastric vein
advancedTest.explain: Splenic outflow is diverted through the short gastric veins, producing isolated fundal varices. Oesophageal varices reflect generalised portal hypertension.

advancedTest.q: Dividing the left gastric artery at its origin during D2 gastrectomy risks liver ischaemia mainly when:

The short gastric arteries are absent or small
The right gastric artery arises from the proper hepatic artery
The gastroduodenal artery comes from the SMA
advancedTest.explain: An aberrant left hepatic artery, found in roughly 10–20% of people, can supply part of the liver, so ligating the left gastric would devascularise it.

advancedTest.q: Why is the stomach notably tolerant of ligation of several named arteries?
choices: The pyloric sphincter shunts duodenal blood back upward
It receives blood from both the celiac trunk and the IMA
Gastric mucosa depends on portal venous oxygen delivery
Curvature arcades feed a rich anastomotic submucosal plexus
advancedTest.explain: The arcades along both curvatures pierce the wall and form a redundant submucosal plexus, so blood reaches tissue even when some arteries are tied.

lessons.title: Liver: Lobes, Couinaud Segments and the Porta Hepatis

levels.kid:
Your **liver** is the biggest organ inside your body. It sits in the upper right part of your belly, tucked under your ribs like a soft, reddish-brown wedge.

The liver is like a busy factory. It cleans your blood, stores fuel for later, and makes a juice called bile that helps you digest fat.

Doctors split the liver into eight sections, like slices of a pizza. Each slice gets its own blood pipe and its own drain pipe. That means a surgeon can take out one sick slice and leave the rest working.

Under the liver there is a special doorway called the **porta hepatis**. Big pipes go in and out there, like trucks at a factory gate.

The liver can even grow back after part of it is removed!
levels.hs:
The **liver** is the largest internal organ. In adults it weighs about 1.5 kg. It sits mostly in the right upper abdomen, under the diaphragm and protected by the lower ribs.

From the outside it looks like it has two main **lobes**, right and left, separated at the front by the **falciform ligament**. On its underside you can also see two small lobes:
- the **quadrate lobe**, in front, next to the gallbladder
- the **caudate lobe**, at the back, next to the inferior vena cava

Surgeons use a more useful map. The **Couinaud classification** divides the liver into **eight segments**. Each one has its own branch of blood supply and its own bile drainage, so each segment works almost like a separate mini-liver.

The **porta hepatis** is a slit on the underside of the liver. Three main structures pass through it:
- the **hepatic portal vein**, which brings nutrient-rich blood from the gut
- the **hepatic artery proper**, which brings oxygen-rich blood
- the **hepatic ducts**, which carry bile out

The liver is unusual because it gets blood from two sources. About 75% comes through the portal vein and about 25% through the hepatic artery. Blood leaves through the **hepatic veins**, which drain into the inferior vena cava.

Example: a surgeon removing a tumor confined to one segment can take out just that segment.
levels.college:
**Surface anatomy and peritoneal attachments.** The liver lies under the right dome of the diaphragm. Most of it is covered by visceral peritoneum. The exception is the **bare area**, a region on the posterior surface that touches the diaphragm directly. The bare area is outlined by the **coronary ligaments**, which extend sideways as the right and left **triangular ligaments**. At the front, the **falciform ligament** carries the **ligamentum teres**, the remnant of the fetal umbilical vein, in its free edge. On the underside, the **fissure for the ligamentum venosum** marks the remnant of the ductus venosus.

**Anatomic vs functional lobes.**
- In anatomic terms, the falciform ligament separates a large right lobe from a smaller left lobe.
- In functional terms, the true dividing plane is **Cantlie's line**. It runs from the gallbladder fossa back to the IVC, roughly along the **middle hepatic vein**.
- The quadrate lobe (segment IV) therefore belongs to the functional left liver, even though it sits to the right of the falciform ligament.

**Couinaud segments.** The liver has eight segments, numbered clockwise when viewed from the front:
- **I**: the caudate lobe
- **II and III**: left lateral section
- **IV** (IVa and IVb): left medial section
- **V–VIII**: right liver; V and VIII form the anterior section, VI and VII the posterior section

Three hepatic veins (right, middle and left) run between sections. The **portal triads** (a portal vein branch, a hepatic artery branch and a bile duct) run into the center of each segment. The plane of the portal bifurcation separates the upper segments from the lower ones.

**Porta hepatis.** This transverse fissure, about 5 cm long, contains, from front to back: the hepatic ducts, the hepatic artery proper branches, and the portal vein. It is enclosed by the **hepatoduodenal ligament**, the free edge of the lesser omentum. Lymphatics and hepatic plexus nerves also enter here.

**Caudate peculiarity.** Segment I receives inflow from both the left and right portal systems. It drains directly into the IVC through short veins.
levels.phd:
**Glisson's capsule and the sheath system.** Glisson's capsule is a fibrous layer that covers the liver. At the hilum it continues inward as sheaths around the portal triads. Couinaud's original work, published in 1957 and based on corrosion casts, defined the segments by portal venous territories. The hepatic veins are intersegmental: they run between segments, not into them. Takasaki later described a "Glissonean pedicle" scheme with three secondary pedicles (left, middle and right). Extrahepatic control of these pedicles allows segment-oriented resections without dissecting each structure separately.

**Brisbane 2000 terminology.** The International Hepato-Pancreato-Biliary Association (IHPBA) standardized the vocabulary for liver anatomy and resections:
- first order: right and left **hemiliver**
- second order: **sections**; on the right, anterior (V and VIII) and posterior (VI and VII); on the left, lateral (II and III) and medial (IV)
- third order: **segments**

This replaced inconsistent older terms such as "lobectomy."

**Variation.** "Classic" textbook patterns hold only partly:
- **Hepatic arterial anatomy** (Michels' classification) is the standard type in roughly 55–75% of people. A replaced right hepatic artery from the superior mesenteric artery occurs in about 10–20%. A replaced left hepatic artery from the left gastric artery occurs in about 10%.
- **Portal vein variants** include trifurcation and a right posterior branch arising from the main portal trunk.
- **Accessory inferior right hepatic veins**, larger than 5 mm, appear in about 10–20% of livers and can drain segment VI directly into the IVC.

**Segmental anatomy as a construct.** Strict eight-segment boundaries are a simplification. Studies of three-dimensional casts show that portal territories vary. Some authors, including Fasel, argued that the number of third-order portal branches is often 20 or more. This challenges the idea of fixed segment boundaries.

**Hilar plate.** The hilar plate is a fusion of connective tissue above the hepatic duct confluence. Lowering this plate exposes the left hepatic duct, which runs a long extrahepatic course under segment IV. This anatomy underpins hilar dissection for perihilar tumors.

**Hepatic arterial buffer response.** When portal inflow falls, adenosine accumulates and dilates the hepatic arterioles. This reciprocal regulation explains why the artery partly compensates for reduced portal flow.
levels.expert:
**Resection planning.** Safe liver surgery depends on the **future liver remnant (FLR)**: the volume of liver left behind. Commonly cited minimums, measured on CT volumetry, are:
- about 20–25% in a normal liver
- about 30% after chemotherapy
- about 40% in cirrhosis

When the remnant is too small, **portal vein embolization** of the side to be removed induces hypertrophy of the remnant over several weeks. Another option is **ALPPS**: the liver is partitioned and the portal vein ligated in a first stage, giving faster growth, but early series reported greater morbidity. **Liver venous deprivation**, which combines portal and hepatic vein embolization, is a newer alternative.

**Intraoperative pitfalls.**
- During left hepatectomy, the middle and left hepatic veins frequently join as a common trunk before entering the IVC. This makes the trunk vulnerable during dissection.
- The **Pringle maneuver** clamps the hepatoduodenal ligament. It controls arterial and portal inflow but not backflow from the hepatic veins. Bleeding that persists despite clamping suggests hepatic venous or IVC injury, or a replaced left hepatic artery running in the lesser omentum.
- Intraoperative ultrasound remains essential for tracing hepatic veins and defining segment planes. **Indocyanine green fluorescence** can stain segments for anatomic resection, by either positive or negative staining.

**Imaging and pathology.**
- Radiologists localize lesions by segment. The plane of the portal bifurcation on axial imaging separates the upper segments (VIII and VII) from the lower ones (V and VI).
- In Budd-Chiari syndrome, the hepatic veins are blocked, but the caudate lobe drains directly into the IVC. The caudate therefore often enlarges.
- In cirrhosis, the caudate and lateral left segments hypertrophy while segment IV and the right posterior section shrink. This is reflected in the caudate-to-right-lobe ratio.

**Transplantation.**
- **Split-liver grafts** typically divide one liver into a left lateral graft (segments II–III), often given to a child, and an extended right graft.
- In **living-donor right lobe donation**, a key decision is whether to reconstruct segment V and VIII venous drainage. These segments drain via the middle hepatic vein; without reconstruction, the graft can become congested.

**Open questions.** Open issues include how to predict regeneration capacity beyond simple volume, for example using functional imaging such as hepatobiliary scintigraphy. Another is whether "anatomic" resection along true portal territories improves cancer outcomes in hepatocellular carcinoma. Evidence on that question is mixed.

keyPoints: The liver gets about 75% of its blood from the portal vein and 25% from the hepatic artery
Cantlie's line (along the middle hepatic vein) divides the functional right and left liver
Couinaud: 8 segments, each with its own portal triad inflow and bile drainage
Segment I is the caudate lobe, which drains directly into the IVC
The porta hepatis transmits the hepatic ducts, hepatic artery and portal vein
Portal triads run into segments; hepatic veins run between them

test.q: Roughly what fraction of the liver's blood supply arrives through the portal vein?
test.explain: About 75% of hepatic inflow is portal venous blood; the hepatic artery supplies about 25%.

test.q: Cantlie's line runs between the gallbladder fossa and which structure?
test.explain: Cantlie's line runs from the gallbladder fossa to the IVC, roughly along the middle hepatic vein, and splits the functional hemilivers.

test.q: Couinaud segment I corresponds to the:
test.explain: Segment I is the caudate lobe. The quadrate lobe is segment IVb.

test.q: Functionally, the quadrate lobe belongs to which part of the liver?
test.explain: The quadrate lobe is segment IV, the left medial section. It sits right of the falciform ligament but left of Cantlie's line.

test.q: Which structure runs between Couinaud segments rather than into their centers?
test.explain: Hepatic veins are intersegmental. The portal triad structures enter the center of each segment.

test.q: The ligamentum teres in the falciform ligament is a remnant of the fetal:
test.explain: The ligamentum teres is the obliterated umbilical vein. The ductus venosus becomes the ligamentum venosum.

test.q: The region of liver touching the diaphragm with no peritoneal covering is the:
test.explain: The bare area is outlined by the coronary ligaments and lies directly against the diaphragm.

test.q: Which peritoneal fold encloses the structures heading to the porta hepatis?
test.explain: The hepatoduodenal ligament, the free edge of the lesser omentum, carries the portal vein, hepatic artery proper and bile duct.

test.q: Why does the caudate lobe often enlarge in Budd-Chiari syndrome?
choices: It is covered by the bare area
It lacks any portal venous inflow
It receives extra hepatic artery blood
It drains directly into the IVC
test.explain: Short caudate veins bypass the blocked main hepatic veins, so the caudate keeps draining and hypertrophies.

test.q: The Couinaud classification divides the liver into ___ functional segments.
test.explain: Segments I to VIII each have independent inflow and biliary drainage.

test.q: What is the name of the transverse fissure on the liver's underside where the portal vein and hepatic artery enter?
test.explain: The porta hepatis is the liver's hilum.

test.q: Clamping the hepatoduodenal ligament to control inflow is called the ___ maneuver.
test.explain: The Pringle maneuver occludes arterial and portal inflow but not hepatic venous backflow.

kidTest.q: Where is your liver?
choices: Middle of the chest, by the heart
Lower left belly, near the hip
Upper right belly, under the ribs
kidTest.explain: The liver sits in the upper right part of your belly, under your ribs.

kidTest.q: Into how many sections do doctors split the liver?
kidTest.explain: Doctors split it into eight sections, like pizza slices.

kidTest.q: Why is it helpful that each section has its own pipes?
choices: A sick section can be removed alone
It makes the liver much heavier
It lets the liver move around
kidTest.explain: Each slice works on its own, so a surgeon can take out just one.

kidTest.q: What juice does the liver make to help digest fat?
kidTest.explain: The liver makes bile, which helps break down fat.

kidTest.q: The liver is like a busy f _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: The liver does many jobs, like a factory.

advancedTest.q: A tumor lies just right of the falciform ligament in the quadrate lobe. Which resection removes it as a functional unit?
advancedTest.explain: The quadrate lobe is segment IV, the left medial section, despite its position right of the falciform ligament.

advancedTest.q: Bleeding continues during liver transection despite a correctly applied Pringle maneuver. The most likely source is:
advancedTest.explain: The Pringle maneuver occludes inflow in the hepatoduodenal ligament but not hepatic venous or IVC backflow.

advancedTest.q: A right-lobe living-donor graft becomes congested in segments V and VIII. The likely anatomical cause is:
choices: Loss of their middle hepatic vein drainage
advancedTest.explain: Segments V and VIII drain via middle hepatic vein tributaries. Without reconstruction, outflow is impaired and the segments congest.

advancedTest.q: A patient needs an extended right hepatectomy, but CT volumetry predicts too small a remnant. A standard way to increase it is:
advancedTest.explain: Embolizing the portal vein of the side to be removed diverts portal flow and drives hypertrophy of the future liver remnant.

lessons.title: Biliary Tree, Gallbladder and the Hepatocystic Triangle

levels.kid:
Your liver makes a green-yellow juice called **bile**. Bile helps break up fat, a bit like dish soap breaks up grease on a pan.

Bile travels through tiny tubes that join into bigger tubes, like small streams joining into a river. This set of tubes is called the **biliary tree**.

The bile doesn't always go straight to your gut. Some of it waits in a little pear-shaped bag under the liver called the **gallbladder**. When you eat a fatty meal, the gallbladder squeezes and sends bile into your intestine.

Sometimes the bile forms hard little pebbles called **gallstones**. If they cause pain, surgeons can take the gallbladder out. They must be very careful to cut the right tube, so they look for a special triangle first.
levels.hs:
**Bile** is made by liver cells and helps digest fats by breaking big fat droplets into small ones (emulsification). It flows through the **biliary tree**, a branching system of ducts.

The path of bile:
- Tiny channels between liver cells drain into bile ducts.
- These join to form the **right and left hepatic ducts**, which leave the liver at the porta hepatis.
- They unite to form the **common hepatic duct**.
- The **cystic duct** from the gallbladder joins it, forming the **common bile duct**.
- The common bile duct runs behind the duodenum and through the pancreas, joins the pancreatic duct, and empties into the second part of the duodenum at the **major duodenal papilla**.

The **gallbladder** sits in a shallow bed on the underside of the liver. It stores and concentrates bile. After a fatty meal, the duodenum releases the hormone **cholecystokinin (CCK)**, which makes the gallbladder contract.

A real example: **gallstones** are very common. When a stone blocks the cystic duct, the gallbladder becomes inflamed (**cholecystitis**), causing pain under the right ribs. Surgeons often remove it by keyhole surgery (**laparoscopic cholecystectomy**). Before cutting anything, they identify a region called the **hepatocystic triangle** to make sure they divide the cystic duct and cystic artery, not the common bile duct.
levels.college:
**Extrahepatic biliary anatomy.** The right and left hepatic ducts emerge at the porta hepatis and join to form the **common hepatic duct (CHD)**, about 3-4 cm long. The **cystic duct** joins it, usually on the right side, to form the **common bile duct (CBD)**, roughly 7-8 cm long, which runs in the free edge of the **hepatoduodenal ligament**. Within that ligament the classic arrangement is: CBD anterior and to the right, **proper hepatic artery** anterior and to the left, and **portal vein** posterior. The CBD then passes behind the first part of the duodenum, grooves the head of the pancreas, and usually joins the main pancreatic duct to form the **hepatopancreatic ampulla (of Vater)**. This opens on the major duodenal papilla in D2, controlled by the **sphincter of Oddi**.

**Gallbladder.** It has a **fundus**, **body**, **neck** and the cystic duct. The fundus projects near the tip of the right 9th costal cartilage at the midclavicular line, where gallbladder tenderness is tested (**Murphy's sign**). A pouch at the neck (**Hartmann's pouch**) is a common site for stones to lodge. The cystic duct contains spiral mucosal folds (the **spiral valves of Heister**).

**Blood supply.** The **cystic artery** usually arises from the **right hepatic artery**. Cystic veins drain mostly directly into the liver bed.

**Triangles.** The **hepatocystic triangle** is bounded by:
- the cystic duct,
- the common hepatic duct,
- the inferior surface of the liver.

Calot's original description (1891) used the cystic artery as the upper border; this smaller area is the true **cystohepatic triangle of Calot**. The hepatocystic triangle contains the cystic artery, often a cystic lymph node (**Lund's node**), and sometimes the right hepatic artery.

**Physiology link.** CCK contracts the gallbladder and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi. Obstruction of the CBD causes **obstructive jaundice** with pale stools and dark urine.
levels.phd:
**Ductal variation is the rule.** The textbook pattern of right and left hepatic ducts joining to form the CHD occurs in only about 57-60% of people. Common variants include a trifurcation and a **right posterior sectoral duct** draining into the left hepatic duct or directly into the CHD. Aberrant right sectoral ducts entering the CHD or cystic duct are especially dangerous because they may run through the hepatocystic triangle and be mistaken for the cystic duct. Small **subvesical ducts** (historically "ducts of Luschka") run in the gallbladder bed and explain some bile leaks after an otherwise uneventful cholecystectomy.

**Cystic duct insertion** varies too. It may be long and run parallel to the CHD, insert medially (spiraling posteriorly), or join low near the duodenum. A parallel cystic duct is a set-up for confusing the CHD with the cystic duct.

**Arterial variation.** The right hepatic artery normally passes posterior to the CHD, but it runs anterior in a meaningful minority of people. It may also arise from the **superior mesenteric artery** (a replaced right hepatic artery, around 10-15% in many series) and then run in or near the triangle. A tortuous right hepatic artery looping close to the gallbladder (the **Moynihan's hump** or caterpillar hump) can be mistaken for the cystic artery. Double cystic arteries also occur.

**Bile duct blood supply** explains ischemic strictures. The supraduodenal CBD is supplied by axial arteries at about the **3 and 9 o'clock positions**, fed mostly from below (gastroduodenal and retroduodenal arteries, roughly 60%) and less from above (right hepatic artery, about 38%), per Northover and Terblanche (1979). Over-dissection around the duct devascularizes it.

**Sphincter of Oddi** has separate muscle bundles around the distal CBD, the pancreatic duct and the ampulla. The union of the CBD and pancreatic duct varies: a common channel, a double-barrel arrangement, or separate openings. An abnormally long common channel (**pancreaticobiliary maljunction**) permits pancreatic juice reflux and is associated with choledochal cysts and gallbladder cancer. Gallstone pancreatitis relates to transient obstruction at this common channel (Opie's 1901 hypothesis).
levels.expert:
**Bile duct injury (BDI)** during laparoscopic cholecystectomy occurs in roughly 0.3-0.5% of cases, about double the open-era rate. The classic injury, described by Strasberg, is **misidentification**: the CBD is taken for the cystic duct, clipped and divided, often with injury to the right hepatic artery. The cause is usually perceptual, not technical. Surgeons who believe they have seen the cystic duct rarely revise that belief, even when the anatomy is inflamed.

**Critical View of Safety (CVS)**, introduced by Strasberg in 1995, prevents this by requiring three criteria before clipping:
- the hepatocystic triangle is cleared of fat and fibrous tissue (the CHD and CBD need not be exposed),
- the lower third of the gallbladder is separated from the liver bed (cystic plate),
- exactly two structures, and only those, are seen entering the gallbladder.

The 2020 multisociety SAGES-led guidelines endorse CVS and recommend documenting it with photos or video. Audits show true CVS is often claimed but not achieved.

**Landmarks and bail-outs.** **Rouvière's sulcus** on the right lobe marks the plane of the CBD; dissection should stay above (ventral to) it. In a severely inflamed **frozen** hepatocystic triangle, where CVS cannot be reached, guidelines favor bail-out strategies over persistence: **subtotal cholecystectomy** (fenestrating or reconstituting) or a fundus-first approach. **Mirizzi syndrome**, where a stone in Hartmann's pouch compresses or erodes into the CHD, is a key reason the triangle can disappear.

**Imaging adjuncts.** Intraoperative cholangiography and **near-infrared fluorescence cholangiography** with indocyanine green (excreted into bile) can show ductal anatomy before dissection. Randomized data show better visualization of extrahepatic ducts, but proving a lower BDI rate would need very large trials. This remains an open question.

**Classification and repair.** Strasberg (A-E) and Bismuth (for strictures) classifications guide management. Complete transection is usually repaired by **Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy** at a specialist center. Outcomes are worse with concurrent vascular injury, early repair in an inflamed field, or repair by the original surgeon. Early referral matters more than speed.

For a future neurosurgeon, the principle carries over: confirm anatomy before dividing anything that cannot be replaced.

keyPoints: Right and left hepatic ducts form the common hepatic duct; adding the cystic duct forms the common bile duct
The CBD runs in the hepatoduodenal ligament and opens at the major papilla in D2 via the ampulla of Vater
The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile; CCK makes it contract
Hepatocystic triangle: cystic duct, common hepatic duct, inferior liver surface; contains the cystic artery
Ductal and arterial variations are common and cause bile duct injuries
The Critical View of Safety reduces misidentification injury during cholecystectomy

test.q: Which two ducts join to form the common bile duct?
test.explain: The cystic duct joins the common hepatic duct to form the CBD. The right and left hepatic ducts form the common hepatic duct, not the CBD.

test.q: Which hormone triggers gallbladder contraction after a fatty meal?
test.explain: CCK, released by the duodenum in response to fats, contracts the gallbladder and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi. Gastric inhibitory peptide mainly enhances insulin release. Pancreatic polypeptide and vasoactive intestinal peptide tend to relax the gallbladder rather than contract it.

test.q: Where does the common bile duct usually empty?
test.explain: It opens at the major duodenal papilla in D2, usually together with the pancreatic duct.

test.q: Which structure forms a boundary of the hepatocystic triangle?
test.explain: The boundaries are the cystic duct, the common hepatic duct and the inferior surface of the liver.

test.q: The cystic artery most commonly arises from the:
test.explain: The usual origin is the right hepatic artery, which is why that artery is at risk in the triangle.

test.q: In the hepatoduodenal ligament, the portal vein lies:
choices: Inside the common bile duct wall
Posterior to the duct and artery
test.explain: The CBD is anterior-right, the proper hepatic artery anterior-left, and the portal vein posterior.

test.q: Why is cholecystectomy risky when the hepatocystic triangle is inflamed?
choices: The cystic artery stops supplying the gallbladder
The gallbladder grows larger than the whole liver
The CBD is easier to mistake for the cystic duct
Bile production by the liver stops during attacks
test.explain: Inflammation hides anatomy, making misidentification of the CBD as the cystic duct more likely, which is the classic injury.

test.q: Murphy's sign tests tenderness at the:
test.explain: The fundus projects near the right 9th costal cartilage at the midclavicular line, where Murphy's sign is elicited.

test.q: A blocked common bile duct typically causes:
test.explain: Bile cannot reach the gut, so stools turn pale while bilirubin enters the urine and darkens it.

test.q: A pouch at the gallbladder neck where stones often lodge is called ___ pouch.
test.explain: Hartmann's pouch is a common site for stone impaction.

test.q: What is the name of the junction of the CBD and pancreatic duct (named after an anatomist)?
test.explain: The hepatopancreatic ampulla (of Vater) opens at the major papilla.

test.q: Keyhole removal of the gallbladder is called laparoscopic ___.
test.explain: Chole = bile, cyst = bladder, ectomy = removal.

kidTest.q: What does bile help your body do?
kidTest.explain: Bile breaks fat into small drops, like soap on a greasy pan.

kidTest.q: Which organ makes bile?
kidTest.explain: The liver makes bile.

kidTest.q: What does the gallbladder do?
kidTest.explain: The gallbladder stores bile until you eat.

kidTest.q: What are gallstones?
kidTest.explain: Bile can form hard little stones.

kidTest.q: The bile tubes join like streams into a river. They are called the biliary t _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Branching tubes make the biliary tree.

advancedTest.q: Bile leaks after a cholecystectomy with secure cystic duct clips. Which structure best explains it?
choices: Subvesical duct in the gallbladder bed
Replaced right hepatic artery near triangle
Major duodenal papilla at the ampulla
Spiral valves of Heister in cystic duct
advancedTest.explain: Subvesical (Luschka) ducts run in the liver bed and can leak once the gallbladder is removed. The valves of Heister are cystic duct folds and do not leak.

advancedTest.q: Why does over-dissecting around the supraduodenal CBD risk later stricture?
choices: It blocks the drainage of the portal vein
It removes the sphincter of Oddi
It devascularizes the 3 and 9 o'clock axial arteries
It disconnects the cystic duct from the CBD
advancedTest.explain: The duct relies on fine axial arteries mostly from below; stripping them causes ischemic stricture.

advancedTest.q: Which CVS criterion most directly guards against a parallel cystic duct mistaken for the CHD?
choices: Staying below Rouvière's sulcus during dissection
Seeing exactly two structures entering the gallbladder
Dividing the cystic artery before the duct
Exposing the common bile duct along its length
advancedTest.explain: Confirming that only two structures enter the gallbladder proves the duct belongs to it. Dissection should stay above Rouvière's sulcus, and exposing the CBD is not required.

advancedTest.q: A long pancreaticobiliary common channel is linked to gallbladder cancer mainly because it allows:
choices: Pancreatic juice reflux into the biliary tree
Bile acids to flood the pancreatic duct
Arterial compression of the cystic duct
Portal blood flow into the bile ducts
advancedTest.explain: With maljunction, the sphincter does not separate the ducts, so pancreatic juice refluxes into bile and injures the epithelium. Bile flowing into the pancreas is the reverse direction.

lessons.title: Pancreas and Spleen: Relations, Ducts and Vessels

levels.kid:
Behind your stomach, tucked against your back, lies a soft organ shaped a bit like a fish lying sideways. It is called the **pancreas**. Its head sits in the curve of your small intestine, and its tail points to the left.

The pancreas has two jobs. It makes juices that help break down food, and it makes **insulin**, which helps your body use sugar.

At the very tip of the tail sits the **spleen**. It is about the size of your fist and hides under your left ribs. The spleen is like a filter for your blood. It catches old, worn-out red blood cells and helps fight germs.

Both organs get blood from a big pipe called the **splenic artery**, which wiggles along the top of the pancreas.
levels.hs:
The **pancreas** is a gland about 15 cm long that lies across the back wall of the abdomen, behind the stomach. Because it sits behind the peritoneum (the lining of the abdominal cavity), it is called **retroperitoneal**. Anatomists describe four parts:
- **Head**: nestled in the C-shaped curve of the duodenum
- **Neck**: in front of the major veins
- **Body**: crossing the spine
- **Tail**: reaching the spleen

The pancreas is both **exocrine** and **endocrine**. Exocrine means it releases digestive enzymes through a duct. Endocrine means it releases hormones like insulin and glucagon straight into the blood. The main pancreatic duct joins the common bile duct and empties into the duodenum.

The **spleen** sits in the upper left abdomen, protected by ribs 9 to 11. It filters blood, removes old red cells and helps the immune system recognise bacteria.

Both organs share a blood supply. The **splenic artery**, a branch of the celiac trunk, runs along the upper edge of the pancreas and sends small branches into it. The **splenic vein** runs just behind the pancreas.

Real example: in a car crash, a blow to the left lower ribs can rupture the spleen and cause dangerous internal bleeding. A seatbelt can crush the pancreas against the spine.
levels.college:
**Pancreas: parts and relations.** The pancreas is secondarily retroperitoneal, except for the tail, which lies in the **splenorenal (lienorenal) ligament** alongside the splenic vessels.
- **Head** lies in the duodenal C-loop, to the right of the superior mesenteric vessels. The **uncinate process** hooks behind the superior mesenteric vein (SMV) and artery (SMA).
- **Neck** lies anterior to the SMV–splenic vein confluence, where the **hepatic portal vein** forms.
- **Body** crosses the aorta and the L1–L2 vertebrae, behind the lesser sac and the stomach.
- **Tail** reaches the splenic hilum.

Posterior to the head lie the inferior vena cava, the right renal vein and the distal common bile duct, which grooves or tunnels through the head.

**Ducts.** The **main pancreatic duct (of Wirsung)** joins the common bile duct at the **hepatopancreatic ampulla (of Vater)**. The ampulla opens at the **major duodenal papilla** in the descending (second) part of the duodenum, controlled by the **sphincter of Oddi**. The **accessory duct (of Santorini)** drains to the **minor papilla**, about 2 cm proximal.

**Arteries.** The gland sits on a watershed between foregut and midgut:
- The head is supplied by the **superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries** (from the gastroduodenal artery, a celiac branch) and the **inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries** (from the SMA). These form anterior and posterior arcades.
- The body and tail are supplied by splenic artery branches: the dorsal pancreatic, **great pancreatic (arteria pancreatica magna)** and caudal pancreatic arteries.

**Spleen.** The spleen is intraperitoneal and lies against ribs 9–11. It is held by the **gastrosplenic ligament** (carrying the short gastric and left gastro-omental vessels) and the splenorenal ligament (carrying the splenic vessels and the pancreatic tail). The tortuous **splenic artery** divides into segmental branches at the hilum, which have few anastomoses between them. The splenic vein receives the **inferior mesenteric vein** (variably), then joins the SMV behind the pancreatic neck.
levels.phd:
**Development explains the ducts.** The pancreas forms from **dorsal and ventral buds** of the foregut endoderm.
- The ventral bud arises with the hepatic diverticulum. It rotates with the duodenum, passing posteriorly to fuse with the dorsal bud.
- The ventral bud forms the inferior head and the uncinate process. The dorsal bud forms the superior head, the neck, the body and the tail.
- The main duct is a composite: the dorsal bud's distal duct fuses with the entire ventral duct. The proximal dorsal duct persists as Santorini's duct.

**Failures of this process:**
- Failure of ductal fusion produces **pancreas divisum**, found in roughly 5–10% of autopsy series. In divisum, most exocrine secretion drains through the minor papilla.
- Abnormal ventral bud migration produces **annular pancreas**, which encircles the second part of the duodenum.

**The spleen's origin.** The spleen is mesodermal, not endodermal. It condenses within the **dorsal mesogastrium**, which divides that mesentery into the gastrosplenic and splenorenal ligaments. When the dorsal mesogastrium fuses with the posterior parietal peritoneum, the pancreas becomes secondarily retroperitoneal.

**Ampullary anatomy varies.** The bile and pancreatic ducts may form:
- a common channel of variable length,
- a shared papilla with separate openings, or
- completely separate openings.

A long common channel (above about 15 mm), called **pancreaticobiliary maljunction**, lies outside sphincter control. It permits reflux of pancreatic juice into the bile duct and is associated with choledochal cysts and biliary cancer.

**Venous anatomy matters surgically.**
- The **first jejunal vein** and the inferior pancreaticoduodenal veins drain into the SMV near the uncinate process.
- The **gastrocolic trunk of Henle** enters the SMV at the inferior border of the neck.
- Behind the neck, the plane between the gland and the SMV–portal vein usually has no anterior tributaries. This makes a **retropancreatic tunnel** possible during pancreatoduodenectomy.

**Splenic microanatomy.** Splenic blood flow is about 5% of cardiac output.
- In the **open circulation**, blood enters the cords of Billroth and must squeeze through endothelial slits to re-enter the sinusoids. This filtering step culls rigid or parasitized erythrocytes.
- Marginal-zone B cells mount T-independent responses to polysaccharide capsules. This explains why loss of the spleen predisposes to **encapsulated organisms**: *S. pneumoniae*, *H. influenzae* and *N. meningitidis*.
levels.expert:
**Pancreatic resection is planned around vessels, not parenchyma.**
- Resectability of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma is graded by tumour contact with the SMA, the celiac axis, the common hepatic artery and the SMV–portal vein.
- Contact above 180° with the SMA or celiac axis generally defines locally advanced disease, although modern neoadjuvant regimens have shifted some patients into resection.
- The "**mesopancreas**" is not a true mesentery. It is the neurolymphatic tissue between the uncinate process and the SMA, and clearing this SMA margin is the major determinant of R0 resection.
- The **replaced right hepatic artery** arises from the SMA in roughly 10–15% of people. It courses behind the head and must be identified on preoperative CT angiography to avoid hepatic ischaemia.

**Pitfalls in pancreatic surgery:**
- The gastroduodenal artery is divided during Whipple procedures. If celiac stenosis exists (for example, from median arcuate ligament compression), hepatic perfusion may depend on retrograde flow through the pancreaticoduodenal arcades. A test clamp of the GDA, with palpation of the hepatic artery pulse, is advised.
- Erosion of the GDA by a posterior duodenal ulcer, or post-pancreatectomy **sentinel bleeds** from GDA stump pseudoaneurysms, are classic causes of catastrophic haemorrhage. They are usually managed by angioembolization.

**The spleen in practice:**
- **Distal pancreatectomy** may preserve the spleen, either by preserving the splenic vessels or by the **Warshaw technique**. The Warshaw technique divides the splenic vessels and relies on the short gastric and left gastro-epiploic collaterals.
- **Splenic trauma** is graded on the AAST scale. Most haemodynamically stable injuries are now managed non-operatively, often with splenic artery embolization. Proximal embolization reduces perfusion pressure while preserving collateral flow.
- **Accessory spleens (splenunculi)** occur in about 10–30% of people, most often at the hilum or in the pancreatic tail. A missed splenunculus can cause relapse after splenectomy for immune thrombocytopenia. An intrapancreatic splenunculus may also mimic a neuroendocrine tumour; technetium-labelled heat-damaged red cell scintigraphy helps resolve the question.

**Splenic vein thrombosis** most often follows pancreatitis. It causes **sinistral (left-sided) portal hypertension** with isolated gastric varices but normal liver function, and splenectomy can be curative.

**Open questions** include how best to prevent postoperative pancreatic fistula, the leading driver of Whipple morbidity, and how reliable radiomic assessment of vascular invasion will prove to be.

keyPoints: Pancreas: head in duodenal C-loop, neck over SMV–portal confluence, body over aorta, tail in splenorenal ligament
Pancreas is secondarily retroperitoneal except its tail; the spleen is intraperitoneal
Main duct (Wirsung) joins the bile duct at the ampulla of Vater, major papilla; accessory duct (Santorini) to minor papilla
Head supplied by superior (celiac via GDA) and inferior (SMA) pancreaticoduodenal arcades
Splenic artery supplies body/tail; splenic vein joins SMV behind the neck to form the portal vein
Spleen held by gastrosplenic and splenorenal ligaments; filters blood and fights encapsulated bacteria

test.q: Which part of the pancreas lies within the C-shaped curve of the duodenum?
test.explain: The head nestles in the duodenal C-loop; the tail reaches the splenic hilum.

test.q: The hepatic portal vein forms behind the pancreatic neck from the union of the splenic vein and the:
choices: Left renal vein at the hilum
test.explain: The SMV and splenic vein join behind the neck to form the portal vein.

test.q: Which ligament carries the splenic vessels and the tail of the pancreas?
test.explain: The splenorenal ligament contains the splenic vessels and the pancreatic tail; the gastrosplenic carries short gastric vessels.

test.q: The main pancreatic duct and common bile duct join at the:
test.explain: They unite at the ampulla of Vater, which opens at the major papilla in the second part of the duodenum.

test.q: The inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries arise from the:
test.explain: Inferior arteries come from the SMA; the superior ones come from the gastroduodenal (celiac) artery.

test.q: Which part of the pancreas hooks behind the superior mesenteric vessels?
test.explain: The uncinate process of the head curls posterior to the SMV and SMA.

test.q: The spleen lies against which ribs on the left side?
test.explain: The spleen lies under left ribs 9–11, which is why lower left rib fractures can injure it.

test.q: The accessory pancreatic duct (of Santorini) drains into the duodenum at the:
test.explain: Santorini's duct opens at the minor papilla, about 2 cm proximal to the major papilla.

test.q: Which statement about peritoneal position is correct?
test.explain: The pancreas is secondarily retroperitoneal except its tail; the spleen is intraperitoneal.

test.q: Which artery, a celiac branch, runs tortuously along the upper border of the pancreas?
test.explain: The splenic artery supplies the pancreatic body and tail en route to the spleen.

test.q: The ampulla of Vater is controlled by the sphincter of ___.
test.explain: The sphincter of Oddi regulates bile and pancreatic juice flow into the duodenum.

test.q: What eponym names the main pancreatic duct?
test.explain: The main duct is the duct of Wirsung; the accessory is Santorini's.

kidTest.q: Where does the pancreas sit?
kidTest.explain: The pancreas is tucked behind the stomach, against the back.

kidTest.q: What does insulin help your body do?
kidTest.explain: Insulin from the pancreas helps the body use sugar.

kidTest.q: What does the spleen do?
kidTest.explain: The spleen filters blood and removes old red cells.

kidTest.q: About how big is the spleen?
kidTest.explain: The spleen is about the size of your fist.

kidTest.q: The spleen hides under your left r _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: The ribs protect the spleen.

advancedTest.q: A patient has pancreas divisum. Through which opening does most pancreatic juice drain, and why?
choices: Major papilla, since the ventral duct drains the tail
Minor papilla, since dorsal bud tissue drains via Santorini
Minor papilla, since the bile duct joins Santorini's duct
Major papilla, since Wirsung's duct fails to form
advancedTest.explain: Without ductal fusion, the large dorsal bud territory (body, tail, upper head) drains via Santorini's duct to the minor papilla.

advancedTest.q: Before dividing the GDA in a Whipple, a surgeon finds celiac stenosis. The main risk is:
choices: Liver ischaemia from loss of retrograde arcade flow
Splenic infarction from loss of short gastrics
Portal vein thrombosis from SMV stasis
advancedTest.explain: With celiac stenosis, hepatic arterial flow may come from the SMA through the pancreaticoduodenal arcades and GDA; dividing it can starve the liver.

advancedTest.q: Isolated gastric varices with normal liver function after pancreatitis most likely reflect:
advancedTest.explain: Splenic vein thrombosis causes sinistral portal hypertension; splenic blood diverts through short gastric veins, forming gastric varices.

advancedTest.q: Why does asplenia predispose to pneumococcal sepsis specifically?
choices: Loss of T-cell priming against intracellular pathogens
Loss of red-cell culling increases iron for bacteria
Loss of marginal-zone B-cell responses to capsules
Loss of platelet storage that limits bacterial spread
advancedTest.explain: Marginal-zone B cells mount T-independent responses to polysaccharide capsules; without them, encapsulated organisms evade clearance.
